outcome: Help merchants place the right inventory by channel and location; benefits include fewer stockouts, lower excess stock, better availability, working-capital release, and explainable planning.
overview: Gulf retailers plan through sharp seasonal swings — Ramadan, back-to-school, White Friday — with promotions, substitutions and long import lead times that spreadsheet planning cannot keep pace with. This solution builds a governed demand layer from POS, e-commerce, ERP and warehouse data, produces SKU-by-location forecasts with explainable drivers, and recommends replenishment within planner-approved constraints. Planners stay in control: every order proposal carries its reasoning and can be adjusted before release to the ERP. An 8–12 week proof of value on selected categories back-tests against the incumbent process, targeting a 10–20% forecast-error improvement, fewer stockouts, lower excess stock and verified working-capital release.

benefits.text: Improve forecast accuracy by a target 10–20% against the incumbent planning process
benefits.source: Redington Retail catalogue; consistent with published AI-forecasting benchmark ranges
benefits.limits: Basis: hypothesis. Target range to validate in a back-test on the customer’s own sales history during the PoV — not a guarantee

benefits.text: Reduce stockouts and excess stock on pilot categories, releasing working capital
benefits.limits: Basis: hypothesis. Depends on SKU/location history quality and lead-time data; measured against an agreed finance baseline

benefits.text: Give planners explainable, adjustable order proposals instead of black-box output
benefits.source: Reference design — planner approval workflow with driver explanations
benefits.limits: Explainability covers model drivers and scenario ranges; benefit depends on planner adoption

residency: Deployable in-country on local AWS or Azure regions (e.g. UAE, KSA); sales and inventory data remain in the customer tenancy in the reference designs

notFor.situation: No SKU/location sales history of at least two seasonal cycles
notFor.why: Seasonal demand models — Ramadan shifts on the lunar calendar — need history that covers the pattern they must learn

notFor.situation: No accountable planning team to review and approve order proposals
notFor.why: The design is planner-in-the-loop; unattended auto-ordering is explicitly out of scope

notFor.situation: Master data too fragmented to join sales, stock and lead times per SKU/location
notFor.why: Forecast and replenishment quality is bounded by the product and location hierarchy beneath it

scope:
Model: Joint delivery: accredited implementation partner leads, with Redington architecture and commercial governance; the customer owns planning policy and replenishment approval · Duration: 8–12 weeks PoV; further 16–28 weeks to enterprise scale
Delivery pod: Partner delivery lead + project manager, forecasting data scientist, integration engineer; customer planning owner, category lead, data owner, ERP administrator, finance reviewer · Support model: Business-hours or 24×7 option; severity-based response targets; partner service desk with vendor escalation
1) Discovery and baseline agreement
2) Data preparation and demand-layer build
3) Model build and historical back-test
4) Planner workbench integration and UAT
5) Training and controlled live comparison
6) Benefit review and handover
